sections.title: Front matter

summary.text: Front matter of the 2017 Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) publication 'Electronic Immunization Registry: Practical Considerations for Planning, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation' (ISBN 978-92-75-11953-2), including copyright and citation metadata, the table of contents, list of acronyms, and preface. It highlights the role of nominal electronic immunization registries (EIRs) in tracking individual vaccination histories across the life course, improving coverage and equity, optimizing EPI management, and supporting vaccine safety and effectiveness research.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION

summary.text: Presents the Introduction (document objectives, target audience, chapter structure in Figure 1, general considerations, and acknowledgments) and opens Chapter 1 on the context of health information systems. It defines health information systems (Section 1.1.2) and outlines the operational and analytical benefits of electronic health information systems (Section 1.1.3), including reduced data entry errors, automated indicator calculation, and geographical disaggregation.

sections.title: Definition of eHealth

summary.text: Presents Section 1.1.1 defining eHealth according to WHO and outlining the six core eHealth components established in PAHO's Strategy and Plan of Action on eHealth (2012–2017) as illustrated in Figure 2: electronic medical records, telehealth, mHealth, eLearning, continuing education in ICTs, and standardization and interoperability.

sections.extract: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), eHealth consists of “the cost- effective and secure use of ICTs in support of health and health-related fields, including healthcare services, health surveillance, health literature, and health education, knowledge and research” [5]. sections.title: Immunization information systems

summary.text: Covers Section 1.1.4 on immunization information systems, Section 1.2 on the seven-stage lifecycle for developing and implementing a health information system, and Section 1.3 on common reasons electronic health information systems fail, before opening Chapter 2 on individualized immunization registries. It defines what an electronic immunization registry (EIR) is (Section 2.1, with a country case study from Uruguay), compares aggregated, paper-based nominal, and electronic nominal registries (Section 2.2), and summarizes the benefits of EIRs for recipients, EPI performance, management, and research (Section 2.3).

sections.extract: Information systems play a key role in producing the information that will guide the strategic, managerial, and operational decisions of the EPI within each country. The ultimate goal is to have information that fulfills three criteria: quality, coverage, and credibility. This allows the EPI to make decisions aimed at reducing the morbidity and mortality associated with vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs) and to

sections.title: Registration of individuals

summary.text: Presents Section 2.4.1 (and 2.4.1.1) on the registration of individuals in an EIR, emphasizing exhaustive, early inclusion of the entire target population—ideally at birth via links to civil or live-birth registries, newborn BCG/Hepatitis B vaccination, and migration databases—across public, social security, private, and NGO providers so the EIR can serve as an accurate population denominator.

sections.extract: 2.4.1.1. Exhaustive inclusion of all people who are targets of the program, ideally at birth An EIR should allow the inclusion of all people within the age group defined as the target population, regardless of whether they have been vaccinated. summary.text: Presents Section 2.4 summarizing the four core pillars of an ideal EIR in Figure 7 (registration of individuals, registration of vaccination events, reports and individual monitoring, and system characteristics), Figure 8 on multisectoral EIR relationships, a country case study on Peru's child registry, and Section 2.4.1.2 on unique individual identification using national ID numbers, maternal-child links, biometrics, and core demographic variables.

summary.text: Covers Section 2.4.2 on registering vaccination events (administered biologics, all public/private vaccination events, vaccine lot traceability, and ESAVI monitoring, with a Bogotá SINV case study), Section 2.4.3 on reporting and individual monitoring, Section 2.4.4 on system usability, timeliness, flexibility, and confidentiality, and Section 2.5 on assessing readiness to develop an EIR (Table 1). It also spans Chapter 3 Sections 3.1–3.3.4 on strategic and operational planning, defining system scope across functional, geographical, population, and sector dimensions, and assessing existing information systems, human resources, information flows, and IT infrastructure.

sections.title: Financial resources

summary.text: Presents Section 3.3.5 on financial resources for an EIR, outlining key planning questions to evaluate capital and maintenance cost estimates, availability of domestic and external funding across the full system lifecycle, and long-term financial sustainability.

sections.extract: A financial mechanism must guarantee availability of the necessary resources throughout the cycle of the EIR system, from the initial investment to routine system maintenance and updates. The following list of questions can help elucidate this aspect. KEY QUESTIONS ? Does the country have a clear and realistic estimate of the capital cost required for the EIR? What information is available and what is lacking? ?

summary.text: Covers Section 3.4 on mapping current information flows and redesigning business processes using the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM, Figure 11), Section 3.5 on lifecycle cost categories and investment justification (Table 3), and Section 3.6 on managing the transition from non-individualized systems to an EIR, including historical data entry options (Tables 4 and 5). sections.extract: The purpose of information systems is to make processes more effective and efficient. sections.title: Usability

summary.text: Presents Section 5.2.2 on software usability principles (ease of learning, ease of use, flexibility, and sturdiness per ISO 9126) with an example checklist of usability requirements in Table 13, and Section 5.2.3 introducing compatibility and interoperability criteria (Table 14).

sections.extract: Usability establishes the clarity of application design according to ISO 9126 (the international standard for evaluation of software product quality). According to this standard, “usability refers to the capability of a software product to be understood, learned, used, and attractive to the user, when it is used under specified conditions” (Table 13). sections.title: Facing future challenges

summary.text: Covers Chapter 7 on future challenges for EIR sustainability—spanning eHealth policies (Table 19), ICT infrastructure and utilization (Table 20), and advanced data quality and use (Table 21)—Chapter 8 on ethical obligations regarding individualized immunization data collection, informed consent, confidentiality, and secondary use, the bibliographic references, and Annexes 1 through 8 (lessons from failed systems, country readiness self-assessment, variable lists, Honduras case study, EIR evaluation criteria, duplicated record exercises, vaccine schedule validation parameters, and database quality analysis examples).
